newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Franco-German EMU rift threatens EU summit.
newsitem.headline: Franco-German EMU rift threatens EU summit.

text.p: European Union leaders were preparing on Saturday for one of their most contentious summits in years, with the bloc's two main motors, France and Germany, at loggerheads over how to proceed towards monetary union.

The traditional Franco-German alliance, which has powered the Union to the brink of economic and monetary union (EMU), has been damaged by the arrival of a socialist French government which, though committed to a single currency, wants a fundamentally new approach to monetary union.

The Amsterdam summit on Monday and Tuesday was supposed to ratify a stability pact, agreed after tough negotiations between France and Germany at the last EU summit in Dublin in December and designed to impose budgetary discipline on the euro-zone.
The meeting is also expected to agree a new EU treaty, signalling a new Citizens' Europe of security, justice and freedom of movement.
Meeting in Poitiers in western France on Friday, French President Jacques Chirac, Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl failed to patch up a rift over the pact.

Jospin, who swept to power promising more jobs and an end to an austerity programme designed to help France qualify for EMU, insists that growth and jobs must be given the same importance as the stability pact in any Amsterdam deal.

Germany opposes costly job-creation schemes which, it argues, have in the past merely raised inflation and interest rates and failed to cut unemployment. Bonn believes that the way to fight joblessness is through structural reforms.
Both sides on Saturday played down talk of a serious schism, saying that a deal in Amsterdam was possible but would require concessions all round.

"The Germans have understood they must make a step forward if they want things to advance and we have to do the same," French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told reporters after a meeting of French Socialist leaders in Paris.

"Mutual concessions are the very definition of co-operation between two countries. I have the impression things are moving -- it's difficult, but things are moving and I hope we will reach agreement in Amsterdam."

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel and Finance Minister Theo Waigel said they were confident France would support an undiluted stability pact, predicting Jospin would retreat from demands to attach job-creation programmes to the pact.
Waigel, architect of the stability pact, said there was no Franco-German rift over the pact and that Germany was just as committed to fighting unemployment.
"France and Germany will clearly be pulling together on the same rope in Amsterdam," Kinkel told the Welt am Sonntag newspaper.

While French and German officials worked intensively through the weekend to bridge their differences, Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, who hosts the Amsterdam summit, predicted a deal would be struck, but only after lengthy negotiations.
"The meeting will only last two days, but the second day will be a long one," he said as he toured a tented press village near the Dutch Central Bank where the summit will be held.
"I'm still perfectly hopeful it will be possible to come to further solutions. We have presented our (EU) presidency paper...and it is now being discussed in various capitals.
"I think they (France and Germany) moved forward (on Friday) but it all, of course, has to be resolved here."
In Amsterdam, protesters clashed with police when a street protest against hardship wrought by Europe's quest for monetary union turned violent.
Some 150 demonstrators smashed windows, overturned a police vehicle and pelted riot police with stones in the city centre.

Organisers of the European Marches Against Unemployment, Poverty and Social Exclusion said some 35,000 protesters jammed the city's central Dam square and walked through the streets to send a message to EU leaders due here for Monday's summit.
Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt told the Brussels newspaper L'Echo that Belgium would support France's drive to focus the single currency project more on jobs.
Kohl's deputy, parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble told Der Spiegel magazine that any delay in launching the euro could endanger the whole project and cause turbulence on currency markets.

Opposition leader Oskar Lafontaine said rapid introduction of the Euro would ease European unemployment. but an opinion poll of 1,000 Germans found 51 percent opposed to the single currency and only 34 percent backed it.
